r: The Supreme Court alone adjudicates justiciable disputes with finality. No other department or agency (e.g., the Tanodbayan) may review its judgments or declare them ‘unjust’.
f: A losing litigant and her lawyer threatened the Justices with exposure and filed graft charges against them before the Tanodbayan over a decision.
h: Lawyer suspended, litigant held in contempt; the Tanodbayan has no jurisdiction to review the Court’s decisions.
x: Use when an executive or legislative body tries to ‘review’, investigate, or punish a court ruling (e.g., a House probe meant to undo a decision).

sub: III.A Separation of powers (also V.A.8 Appropriations)
r: A law cannot authorize the President to transfer funds indiscriminately. Transfers are allowed only from actual savings, to augment an existing item, within the official’s own branch (now Art. VI, Sec. 25(5)). Where a branch exceeds its authority, the Court must step in.
f: Sec. 44 of PD 1177 let the President transfer any appropriated fund of the Executive to any program or project in the GAA, without regard to savings or augmentation.
h: The first paragraph of Sec. 44 was declared unconstitutional.
x: Use for any law or GAA provision giving the President or a department head a blanket power to realign funds. Pair with Araullo (DAP) and Macalintal (2023).
test: Valid transfer: (1) a law authorizes it; (2) the funds are actual savings; (3) the transfer augments an existing item; (4) within the same branch or office.
s: No blanket authority to transfer funds: actual savings, existing item, own branch (Art. VI, Sec. 25(5)).

r: When the Court allocates constitutional boundaries it does not assert superiority; it performs its duty to settle conflicting claims of authority. Judicial review is limited to actual cases and to the lis mota. The Electoral Commission (now the electoral tribunals) has exclusive power over contests, including setting its own deadline for protests.
f: The National Assembly ‘confirmed’ Angara’s election and set a protest deadline, but the Electoral Commission accepted Ynsua’s protest filed later under its own rules.
h: The Electoral Commission acted within its exclusive jurisdiction; the Assembly’s resolution could not cut it off.
x: Cite for the moderating power of the judiciary, checks and balances, and the independence of electoral tribunals from their chamber.
g: Gatmaytan’s book opens judicial review with Angara’s ‘deft strokes and bold lines’ passage.
s: Judicial review allocates constitutional boundaries; it does not assert judicial supremacy; actual case and lis mota.

r: Where the Constitution imposes conditions (e.g., a plebiscite for converting the status of a local unit, Art. X, Sec. 10), whether they were met is justiciable, not political.
f: RA 8528 downgraded Santiago, Isabela from an independent component city to a component city without providing for a plebiscite.
h: RA 8528 was unconstitutional for lack of a plebiscite; the issue was justiciable.
x: Use to rebut a ‘political question’ defense whenever the Constitution sets a procedural condition on the political branches.
s: Whether constitutional conditions (e.g., a plebiscite) were met is justiciable, not political.

r: Choosing where to build a government project is a question of policy and wisdom, not legality: a political question the Court will not decide absent a constitutional or legal violation.
f: A barangay captain sought to stop the C-5 road extension through the Balara aqueduct area, preferring another route.
h: Petition dismissed; the Court cannot choose the better route.
x: Use when a petition really attacks the wisdom of a project or policy, not its legality.

r: Petitions against the No Contact Apprehension Policy ordinances were dismissed: supervening events (suspension of the ordinances and the Metro Manila Traffic Code of 2023) made them moot, no exception to mootness applied, and most petitioners lacked standing or capacity to sue.
f: Transport groups challenged NCAP ordinances of several Metro Manila cities; the Court issued a TRO in 2022, and the cities later adopted a uniform Traffic Code.
h: Dismissed without prejudice to a future challenge to the new scheme. Unregistered associations lacked capacity to sue; groups claiming third-party standing failed to identify their members or show the members wanted them to sue.
x: A 2026 case: a fresh source for mootness (relief would be ‘illusory’), the four exceptions applied strictly, and third-party standing requirements. Likely to be used against weak procedural pleading.
w: Decided June 3, 2026, with separate opinions (Leonen, Lazaro-Javier, Dimaampao). Details here follow the block digest and the Supreme Court’s July 2026 press briefer; read the decision if time allows.
s: Supervening repeal makes a case moot; exceptions applied strictly; associations must show capacity and members’ consent.

n: White Light Corporation v. City of Manila
r: Exceptions to the direct-injury rule include third-party standing, overbreadth, taxpayer suits, and transcendental importance. Motel owners may assert their patrons’ rights. An ordinance banning ‘short-time’ rates is an unreasonable exercise of police power.
f: A Manila ordinance banned short-time admission and wash-up rates in hotels and motels to curb illicit sex and prostitution.
h: The ordinance was struck down: lawful purpose but unreasonable, overbroad means that intrude on liberty of legitimate patrons.
x: Use for third-party standing and for the police power test (lawful subject plus lawful means). It also shows that an LGU regulation burdening businesses fails when the means are unduly oppressive.
test: Third-party standing: (1) the litigant suffered an injury-in-fact; (2) a close relation to the third party; (3) some hindrance to the third party’s ability to sue.
s: Third-party standing allowed; banning short-time motel rates is unreasonable police power.

r: Mere apprehension that a power may be abused does not create a justiciable controversy; the petitioner must show a present or threatened injury.
f: Private schools challenged a law requiring government permits and inspection, without showing any permit had been revoked or threatened.
h: Dismissed as premature (no justiciable controversy).
x: Use when petitioners attack a regulatory law before any enforcement or threatened enforcement against them.

r: A proposed bill is not subject to judicial review: it is not a law, creates no rights, and a ruling would be an advisory opinion. There is no vested right to public office or to the SK age limits.
f: Youths challenged a bill postponing the SK elections and lowering the age limit, which would make them ineligible.
h: Dismissed: no actual controversy (they agreed to the new date), no standing, and the bill was not yet a law.
x: Use against any challenge to a bill, a pending Charter change resolution, or a ‘proposal’ in the news. Pair with In re JDF and Lozano v. Nograles.
s: A bill is not ripe for review: no rights, no duties, only an advisory opinion.

r: A House resolution merely calling for Congress to convene as a constituent assembly is not ripe. Ripeness: the challenged act must have been accomplished and must have a direct adverse effect on the petitioner.
f: Petitioners assailed House Resolution 1109, which called Congress to convene for proposing constitutional amendments.
h: Dismissed: not ripe, no standing (no disbursement of funds), transcendental importance not applicable.
x: Charter change in the news (a resolution to convene a constituent assembly): the challenge is premature until Congress actually acts.

n: Philippine Constitution Association v. Philippine Government
r: Challenges to the Framework Agreement and Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro were premature: these peace agreements need a law (the BBL) to take effect, and Congress is not bound by them.
f: Petitioners argued the FAB and CAB with the MILF were unconstitutional like the MOA-AD.
h: Dismissed as not ripe. Distinguished from North Cotabato (MOA-AD), where the Executive bound itself to amend the Constitution.
x: Use when the Executive signs an agreement or framework that still needs legislation (peace deals, MOUs).

n: Atlas Fertilizer v. Secretary of DAR
r: A case becomes moot when a supervening event (here, a ruling in another case and an amendatory law) removes the controversy, so that any ruling has no practical use.
f: Aquaculture firms challenged CARL’s coverage of fishponds; Luz Farms and RA 7881 later excluded such lands.
h: Dismissed as moot.
x: Supervening legislation or a ruling in another case makes a challenge moot.

r: Lifting the declaration of a ‘state of rebellion’ made the petitions moot. Fear of warrantless arrest does not justify mandamus or prohibition when ordinary remedies exist.
f: After the May 1, 2001 siege of Malacañang, President Arroyo declared a state of rebellion; opposition figures feared warrantless arrests.
h: Dismissed; the State said it would get regular warrants.
x: Use with Sanlakas for mootness after a proclamation is lifted.

r: Though moot when the proclamation was lifted, the Court ruled because the issue is capable of repetition yet evading review. The President may declare a state of rebellion under her executive and commander-in-chief powers; the declaration adds no new powers. Only the legislator-petitioners had standing.
f: After the 2003 Oakwood mutiny, President Arroyo declared a state of rebellion and called out the AFP, then lifted it.
h: Petitions dismissed; the declaration was valid but legally superfluous.
x: Lists the exceptions to mootness and shows legislative standing (an executive act that impairs congressional power, here emergency powers).
test: A moot case may still be decided if: (1) grave violation of the Constitution; (2) exceptional character and paramount public interest; (3) need to formulate controlling principles for the bench, the bar and the public; (4) capable of repetition yet evading review.
s: Moot but decided: capable of repetition yet evading review; only legislators had standing.

r: Citizens have no standing to stop the auction of property that is neither theirs nor public; there is no taxpayer standing where no public funds are disbursed.
f: Petitioners sought to stop the PCGG’s auction of Old Masters paintings and silverware taken from the Marcoses.
h: Dismissed for lack of standing.
x: Use when petitioners claim a ‘national heritage’ interest in property not shown to be public, or claim taxpayer status with no disbursement.

r: An employees’ association has standing where its members stand to be injured. On the merits, the CHR needed DBM approval to upgrade and collapse positions; it does not have the fiscal autonomy of the constitutional commissions.
f: The CHR upgraded senior positions and collapsed vacant ones, funded from personal services; the DBM disapproved, and the rank-and-file association sued.
h: The association had standing; the upgrading without DBM approval was invalid.
x: Associational standing of employees; limits on ‘fiscal autonomy’ claims by bodies the Constitution does not list.

n: Automotive Industry Workers Alliance v. Romulo
r: Unions without direct injury lack standing to challenge an executive order giving the Labor Secretary administrative supervision over the NLRC. No taxpayer standing without a disbursement of funds. The Court declined to relax the rule.
f: Ten unions assailed EO 185 transferring administrative supervision over the NLRC from its Chairperson to the DOLE Secretary.
h: Dismissed for lack of standing; constitutionality left for a proper party.
x: The cleanest statement of the ‘personal and substantial interest’ test and why courts guard it.

sub: III.D.2 Citizen standing (also effectivity of laws)
r: Citizens may sue to enforce a public right (here, publication of laws) without showing special injury. Laws of general application must be published in the Official Gazette to take effect.
f: Citizens sought mandamus to compel publication of unpublished presidential decrees and issuances.
h: Publication ordered. (The 1986 resolution extended the rule: all statutes, including those of local application and private laws, must be published, 15 days after publication unless the law provides otherwise.)
x: Use for citizen standing and for any IRR, ordinance or rule that took effect without publication.
test: Must be published: statutes, PDs and EOs in the exercise of legislative power, and IRRs that implement laws. Need not: purely interpretative rules, internal rules for agency personnel, letters of instruction to subordinates.
s: Citizens may enforce a public right without special injury; all laws and implementing rules must be published.

r: A citizen has standing to enforce the right to information and the constitutional ban on private corporations acquiring alienable lands of the public domain. Reclaimed submerged lands are public domain; Amari could not own them.
f: PEA agreed to transfer reclaimed Manila Bay lands (Freedom Islands) to Amari, a private corporation.
h: The amended joint venture agreement was void.
x: Citizen standing based on a public right (Art. III, Sec. 7; Art. XII, Sec. 3).
s: Citizen standing to enforce the right to information and the ban on corporations acquiring public lands.

r: A labor group whose members are commuters has standing to challenge fare-setting rules that injure them. The LTFRB cannot delegate rate-fixing power to the operators themselves.
f: DOTC and LTFRB orders let bus operators raise fares within a band without LTFRB approval.
h: The fare-band rules were struck down as undue delegation (the LTFRB cannot redelegate its power).
x: Associational standing, and the rule against subdelegation (delegata potestas non potest delegari).

r: The IBP lacked standing: its interest in the rule of law is too general. The Court nonetheless ruled, given transcendental importance. Calling out the armed forces is a matter of presidential discretion reviewable only for grave abuse.
f: President Estrada deployed Marines to patrol Metro Manila with the PNP to curb crime.
h: Deployment upheld; no grave abuse shown; civilian supremacy not violated.
x: Associational standing must rest on members’ injury, not a general interest; transcendental importance can relax standing.
s: A general interest in the rule of law is not standing; transcendental importance may relax it; calling-out power reviewable for grave abuse.

n: Executive Secretary v. Court of Appeals
r: An association of recruitment agencies may sue for its members since its purpose is to represent them, but it cannot assert the rights of unskilled workers, with whom it has no substantial relation.
f: An association of 11 recruitment agencies challenged penal and other provisions of RA 8042 before it took effect.
h: The association had standing only for its members; the lower court’s injunction was set aside.
x: Limits of associational and third-party standing: there must be a substantial relation to the party whose rights are asserted.

r: Broadcasters have standing to assert their own press freedom and, as third parties, candidates’ free speech and the public’s right to information. COMELEC’s aggregate airtime limits were unconstitutional.
f: COMELEC limited each candidate’s political ads to an aggregate total across all stations.
h: Aggregate-airtime rule struck down.
x: Third-party standing for media; election regulation that burdens speech.

r: Taxpayers have standing when public funds are being disbursed illegally. COMELEC’s award of the automated counting machine contract to an ineligible bidder was void.
f: COMELEC awarded a ₱1.3-billion contract to a consortium that did not qualify and whose machines failed tests.
h: The award and contract were voided.
x: Taxpayer standing requires an illegal disbursement or misuse of public funds.

sub: III.D.2 Voter standing (also V.A.2 Special election)
r: Voters have standing to question the validity of an election. A law fixing the special election simultaneously with the next regular election operates as the call; COMELEC’s failure to give separate notice did not invalidate a Senate special election.
f: After Senator Guingona became Vice President, the 13th-placing senatorial candidate in 2001 was proclaimed for the unexpired term; the vote was not separately canvassed.
h: Special election valid; petition dismissed.
x: Use for voter standing and the special election rules (Senate: with the next regular election; House: 60 to 90 days after the vacancy).
g: Gatmaytan’s book distinguishes House vacancies: there COMELEC must call and give notice, or the special election is void. Read with Hagedorn (2025).
s: Voters have standing to question an election; the law itself can serve as the call for a special election.

r: A senator has standing to challenge an executive act that usurps legislative power. A national ID system cannot be created by administrative order; it requires a law and must respect privacy.
f: President Ramos issued AO 308 establishing a national computerized ID system.
h: AO 308 struck down.
x: Legislative standing: a member of Congress may sue when an executive act encroaches on Congress’s powers.

r: The State (here, the prosecution) may challenge the validity of its own law. The Probation Act unduly delegated legislative power by leaving it to provincial boards to decide whether the law would apply.
f: In the Cu Unjieng case, the prosecution assailed the Probation Act after the trial court entertained a probation application.
h: The Probation Act was declared unconstitutional (undue delegation; equal protection).
x: Governmental standing; also a classic undue-delegation case (no sufficient standard).

n: Resident Marine Mammals v. Secretary Reyes
sub: III.D.2 Standing for future generations and fauna
r: Animals need not be given legal personality to sue: the Rules of Procedure for Environmental Cases let any Filipino citizen, as steward of nature, file a citizen suit. Oil exploration in Tañon Strait without a law was void.
f: Petitions on behalf of dolphins and whales, by their ‘stewards’, challenged a service contract for oil exploration in a protected seascape.
h: Service contract declared null; it lacked a general law and was not reported to Congress.
x: Environmental standing questions: future generations, fauna, citizen suits.
g: Gatmaytan, ‘The Illusion of Intergenerational Equity’: Oposa’s pronouncement on suing for future generations was obiter, not needed to resolve cause of action; it has not done the work celebrated for it.

n: Falcis III v. Civil Registrar General
r: The mere passage of a law does not create an actual case. A facial challenge to the Family Code’s opposite-sex marriage provisions failed: no actual case, no standing (petitioner never applied for a license), wrong respondent, and violation of the hierarchy of courts.
f: A self-identified gay lawyer, who had never applied for a marriage license, asked the Court to void Family Code Arts. 1 and 2.
h: Dismissed. Counsel were also cited for contempt over their attire and conduct.
x: Use against abstract or ‘advocacy’ petitions filed directly with the Supreme Court; the petitioner must have an injury and a real adverse party.
s: Passage of a law alone is no actual case; no injury, wrong respondent, hierarchy of courts.

r: Constitutionality must be raised at the earliest opportunity in the trial court and must be the lis mota of the case. Accused who did not move to quash on that ground cannot go straight to the Supreme Court.
f: Persons charged under BP 22 (bouncing checks) went directly to the Supreme Court to have the law voided.
h: Dismissed: no lis mota, not raised below, hierarchy of courts.
x: Use when a party raises unconstitutionality late or when the case can be decided on other grounds.
